prompt: Lesson 4's nearest-centroid classifier was given the eight odd inbox messages. What did it do with the question about boiling water on Everest?
hint: Look at the label column of forced.py's output.

choices.text: Gave it a label, account, with a score of 0.034
choices.why: Right. A classifier chooses among the labels it was built with; it has no way to answer none of these.

choices.text: Refused it, because the score was below zero
choices.why: Nothing in the classifier refuses. It takes the highest score, however low, and 0.034 is above zero anyway.

choices.text: Put it in a sixth group for unknown messages
choices.why: There is no sixth group. The classifier was built from five labels and can only output those five.

choices.text: Raised an error because the text is not about books
choices.why: The model embeds any text. Nothing checks the subject, which is why the question got a label at all.

prompt: Why does the lesson not train a sixth label, odd, from the eight odd messages and add it to the classifier?
hint: Read the eight messages side by side.

choices.text: Eight examples are too few for any classifier to learn from
choices.why: Lesson 4's centroids were built from 20 examples a label and worked. Small numbers are not the main obstacle here.

choices.text: A label needs exactly as many examples as the others
choices.why: Classifiers can learn from unbalanced labels. The problem is what the examples have in common, not how many there are.

choices.text: They share nothing, and next week's odd ones will differ
choices.why: Right. Spam, French, noise and a CV are not one category, so a label trained on them would learn these eight and miss the next ones.

choices.text: Odd messages cannot be embedded by an English model
choices.why: They can: every one of them got a vector and a score. Only two are in other languages, and even those get vectors.

prompt: Anomaly detection with embeddings turns the question around: embed the messages known to be ___, and score each new message by its distance from the region they occupy.
hint: The 150 tickets are examples of it.

prompt: centroid.py scores a message as one minus its cosine with the centroid. What does a score of 0 mean?
hint: Cosine is 1 for the same direction.

choices.text: It points the way the average ticket points
choices.why: Right. A cosine of 1 gives a score of 0, and the score grows as the message turns away from the centroid.

choices.text: The message has nothing to do with any ticket
choices.why: That is the other end: unrelated texts have a cosine near 0, so a score near 1.

choices.text: The message is an exact copy of one of the tickets
choices.why: A copy of one ticket matches that ticket, not the average of 150. Its score against the centroid would be well above 0.

choices.text: The score could not be computed
choices.why: 0 is an ordinary score here. Nothing in the program signals failure with it.

prompt: The mean of the 150 ticket vectors, each of length 1, has a length of 0.425. What does that say about the tickets?
hint: When would the mean of unit vectors have length 1?

choices.text: The model returned vectors shorter than 1 for some tickets
choices.why: Every all-MiniLM-L6-v2 vector has length 1. The shortening happens in the averaging, not in the model.

choices.text: They point in several different directions
choices.why: Right. Vectors pointing the same way would average to length 1; five kinds of ticket pull the mean in five directions and it shrinks.

choices.text: A quarter of the tickets are near-duplicates of each other
choices.why: Duplicates point the same way, which keeps the mean long. The short mean comes from spread, not from repetition.

choices.text: The centroid cannot be used until it is made longer than 1
choices.why: It is divided by its length to get back to 1, but that is a convenience: the ranking by cosine would be the same either way.

prompt: Two unit vectors are at right angles to each other (their dot product is 0). What is the length of their mean, to three decimal places?
hint: The mean is (a + b) / 2. Its squared length is (1 + 0 + 0 + 1) / 4.

prompt: Against the centroid, the free-iPhone spam (m33) came 16th, below eight normal messages. Which explanation does the lesson give?
hint: Where does the centroid sit relative to the five groups?

choices.text: Spam is always written to look like a customer message
choices.why: Most of the spam in the inbox scored high. The issue is where the centroid sits, not a property of spam in general.

choices.text: The centroid lies between the five groups, where no ticket is
choices.why: Right. Distance to the average of five topics is not distance to any one of them, and the spam scored 0.321 against the returns centroid.

choices.text: m33 is longer than the other odd messages, and long texts score lower
choices.why: Length does not move a score here: every vector has length 1, whatever the text.

choices.text: The model was trained on spam, so it treats spam as normal
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says what the model was trained on beyond English pairs, and a model does not flag or pass anything; the score does.

prompt: Order these inbox messages as centroid.py ranked them, from the highest score (furthest from normal) down.
hint: The Everest question scored above 1.
items: What is the boiling point of water at the top of Mount Everest?
Meu pedido ainda não chegou e já faz duas semanas, alguém pode me ajudar?
Je n'arrive pas à me connecter à mon compte depuis ce matin.
Can you recommend a good recipe for vegetable lasagne?
trap: The Portuguese message scored above the French one, though both are in a language the model does not know.

prompt: With k=5, what is a message's score in knn.py?
hint: Sort its similarities to the tickets.

choices.text: One minus its similarity to the fifth most similar ticket
choices.why: Right. The k-th largest similarity is the k-th nearest ticket, and one minus it is the distance.

choices.text: The mean distance to every ticket
choices.why: That would compare against all 150 at once, which is close to what the centroid does. k=5 looks at one particular neighbour.

choices.text: The share of its five nearest tickets that are odd
choices.why: The reference contains only normal tickets, so there is nothing odd to count. The score is a distance, not a vote.

choices.text: Its distance to the centroid of the five ticket labels
choices.why: The labels play no part in knn.py. Five is the k, not the number of categories.

prompt: After one spam message was added to the normal set, m33 fell to 20th with k=1 but stayed 9th with k=5. Why the difference?
hint: Which neighbour does each k look at?

choices.text: k=5 ignores any message that looks like spam
choices.why: Neither score knows what spam is. They differ only in which neighbour they measure.

choices.text: Adding a message changes the model, and k=5 is less affected
choices.why: The model does not change. Only the reference set changed, by one vector.

choices.text: The planted spam became its single nearest neighbour
choices.why: Right. One bad message in the reference can hide its look-alikes from k=1; a larger k needs several before it is fooled.

choices.text: k=5 scores are always higher, so m33 stays near the top
choices.why: Higher scores for everyone do not change a rank by themselves. m33 kept its rank because its own fifth neighbour stayed far.

prompt: Marginalia's reference grows to a million normal tickets. How does the cost of scoring one new message change for each method?
hint: Count the comparisons each one makes.

choices.text: Both stay the same, because a vector has 384 numbers whatever the reference size
choices.why: The vector size is fixed, but the number of vectors compared is not, for one of the methods.

choices.text: The centroid grows with the reference and the nearest neighbours do not
choices.why: The other way round: the centroid is computed once and is a single vector to compare with.

choices.text: The centroid stays one comparison; the nearest neighbours need a million, or an index
choices.why: Right. k-nearest-neighbour scoring is a vector search over the reference, which is what lessons 11 to 15 make fast.

choices.text: Both grow, but the centroid grows faster because the mean is recomputed
choices.why: The mean is computed once when the reference is built, not for every message scored.

prompt: Put the steps of computing a message's k-nearest-neighbour score in order.
hint: The reference is embedded before anything is compared with it.
items: Embed the normal messages once, as the reference
Take its dot product with every reference vector
Sort those similarities and take the k-th largest
Subtract it from 1 to get the score
trap: Sorting comes after the dot products, not before: there is nothing to sort until every similarity exists.

prompt: Why does threshold.py score the 50 test tickets against the 100 training tickets instead of scoring all 150 against themselves?
hint: Look at the first line of its output.

choices.text: Scoring 150 against 150 is too slow
choices.why: It is 22,500 dot products, which takes no time at all. Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Each ticket would find itself
choices.why: Right. The first line shows a highest score of 0.000. A cut-off read from those scores would flag almost everything.

choices.text: The test tickets are odd and the training ones are normal
choices.why: All 150 tickets are normal. The test ones are held out so that they are normal messages the reference has not seen.

choices.text: Lesson 4 used the test tickets up, so they cannot be in the reference
choices.why: Nothing is used up. They are kept out of the reference here for the same reason lesson 4 kept them out of training.

prompt: The cut-off is set at the 95th percentile of the held-out normal scores. What does that promise?
hint: A percentile describes the data it was read from.

choices.text: 95% of the odd messages that arrive will be caught
choices.why: The percentile was read from normal messages only. How many odd ones get caught can only be measured with known odd messages.

choices.text: Exactly 5% of all of tomorrow's messages will be flagged
choices.why: Tomorrow's flags depend on how many odd messages arrive. And even for normal ones it is roughly one in twenty, not exactly.

choices.text: About one normal message in twenty lands above it
choices.why: Right. That is the false-alarm rate it was chosen for; it says nothing about recall.

choices.text: A score above it is at least 95% likely to be odd
choices.why: A score is not a probability, as lesson 2 said. The percentile is a position among normal scores.

prompt: With k=5 at the 90th percentile, threshold.py flagged 11 messages, and 8 of them were odd. What is the precision, as a fraction with two decimals?
hint: Precision is odd flagged divided by all flagged.

prompt: With k=5 at the 99th percentile, threshold.py missed m33 and m37 and flagged nothing by mistake. There are 8 odd messages. What is the recall, as a fraction with two decimals?
hint: Recall is odd flagged divided by all odd.

prompt: Match each term to what it counts on the inbox.
hint: Two of them are rates, two are single messages.

pairs.right: Of the flagged messages, the share that were odd
Of the odd messages, the share that were flagged
A normal message above the line
An odd message below the line

right_distractors: Of all messages, the share that were normal

prompt: In week 2, only four of the twenty messages crossed the cut-off. Why does the lesson still say the inbox changed?
hint: Look at the batch numbers rather than the flags.

choices.text: Four flags in a day is above the 5% the threshold allows
choices.why: The threshold's 5% is about normal messages in general, and four of twenty is not a test of it. The batch numbers are the evidence.

choices.text: The mean rose, and 11 of 20 were nearest each other
choices.why: Right. The batch moved away from the reference, and its messages resemble each other more than anything known: a new topic.

choices.text: The four flagged messages were spam disguised as subscription questions
choices.why: They were real customers asking about the subscription. None of week 2's messages is spam.

choices.text: The model was updated between the two weeks
choices.why: The same model scored both weeks. What changed was what customers wrote about.

prompt: A cut-off is read from the scores of normal messages that the reference never saw, which the lesson calls ___ data.
hint: The 50 test tickets were kept out of the reference for this.

prompt: When the data a system sees moves away from the data it was built on, as week 2's inbox did, it is called ___.
hint: A word for slowly moving away from a course.

prompt: To stop the subscription questions setting off the detector, a colleague proposes putting everything received each day into the reference, automatically. What is the risk?
hint: What happened to k=1 when one spam message was in the reference?

choices.text: The reference grows and scoring becomes slower
choices.why: It does grow, and that is a cost, but it is not the danger. The danger is what the reference then calls normal.

choices.text: Spam that gets in once becomes normal, and its look-alikes stop being flagged
choices.why: Right. Anything in the reference stops being flagged, which is how one planted spam hid m33 from k=1. Add messages somebody has read.

choices.text: The model has to be retrained every day
choices.why: Nothing retrains the model. The reference is a list of vectors, and adding to it changes no weights.

choices.text: The threshold stops being a percentile
choices.why: The threshold can be read again from held-out data at any time. The problem is what was let into the reference.

prompt: A refund request for 4,800 on order 1182 scored well under the cut-off. Why could the detector not flag it?
hint: What does an embedding capture best, according to lesson 1?

choices.text: The amount has a comma, which the model ignores
choices.why: Punctuation is not the issue. Even written without the comma, an amount is not something the vectors compare.

choices.text: Refund requests are excluded from scoring
choices.why: Every message is scored the same way. This one scored low because it reads like the refund tickets.

choices.text: Its subject is an ordinary refund, and the vector does not weigh amounts
choices.why: Right. The detector measures distance of subject, and the suspicious part is a number inside a normal subject.

choices.text: The threshold was set too high on purpose to avoid false alarms
choices.why: No line in the k=1 table would flag it: it sits among the normal scores, not just above them.

prompt: The same late-order complaint passes in English and is flagged in Portuguese. What is the flag really reporting?
hint: Only one thing differs between the two versions.

choices.text: That Portuguese-speaking customers write more unusual complaints
choices.why: The two messages say the same thing. Only the language differs, and so only the language explains the flag.

choices.text: That the message is spam written in Portuguese to avoid filters
choices.why: It is an ordinary complaint about a late order, and its English version passes.

choices.text: A fault in the threshold, which should be lower for other languages
choices.why: Moving the line would not fix it: the Portuguese vector is far from the shipping tickets because the model cannot read it.

choices.text: That the model was trained on one language only
choices.why: Right. The anomaly belongs to the model, as lesson 1's −0.015 showed; a multilingual model would pass it.

prompt: A bank wants to detect fraudulent transfer requests in its support chat with this lesson's method, scoring each message against a year of normal chats. What will it catch and miss?
hint: Ask whether the fraud changes the subject of the message.

choices.text: It will catch fraud, since fraudulent requests are rare and rare means far from normal
choices.why: Rare in the bank's records does not mean far in meaning. A fraudulent transfer request reads like any transfer request.

choices.text: Off-topic chats caught; fraud phrased normally passes
choices.why: Right. The detector measures subject. Fraud inside a normal subject needs checks on amounts, accounts and history.

choices.text: It will catch nothing, because a bank's chats are too varied for a reference
choices.why: Variety is what k-nearest-neighbour scoring handles: several groups, each with near neighbours. Off-topic chats would still stand out.

choices.text: It will catch everything once the threshold is set at the 99th percentile
choices.why: A higher line only flags fewer messages. No position of the line sees an amount.

prompt: Ana's detector scores messages by k=1 distance to the normal tickets, with an English-only model. Which of these would it flag? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask whether each one changes the subject, or the language, rather than the details.

choices.text: A message asking for a pasta recipe
choices.why: Yes. A recipe question has no near neighbour among the tickets, like the lasagne message in the inbox.

choices.text: A delivery complaint written in Spanish
choices.why: Yes, for the model's reasons: an English model cannot place Spanish near the shipping tickets, as with the Portuguese complaint.

choices.text: A refund request for an amount twenty times the order total
choices.why: No. It is an ordinary refund request by subject, and the vector does not weigh the amount.

choices.text: A request to send the account's password to a new address
choices.why: No. It reads as an account question, which is a normal subject, however dangerous the request is.

prompt: Match each choice from the lesson to the weakness it showed on Marginalia's data.
hint: One weakness belongs to no choice.

pairs.right: Missed the spam, which sat near the middle of five groups
Fooled by one spam message slipped into the reference
A narrower gap between the last odd and the first normal message

pairs.left: A cut-off picked from today's scores
pairs.right: Looks good only on the messages it was picked from

right_distractors: Cannot rank the messages at all
